objectives: Reason about why QUIC runs on UDP.

slides.title: Why QUIC was designed
slides.body:
TCP and TLS were designed in the 1970s and 1980s — an era of wired, stable, low-latency networks. By the 2010s, mobile clients, lossy wireless links, and latency-sensitive applications revealed three structural weaknesses.

**1. Head-of-line (HoL) blocking in HTTP/2.** HTTP/2 (RFC 7540, 2015) introduced stream multiplexing: many logical request/response streams share a single TCP connection, eliminating the need to open multiple parallel connections. But TCP is a byte-stream protocol — it delivers bytes in strict order. A single dropped packet somewhere in the stream forces ALL multiplexed streams to stall and wait for the retransmission, even streams with no relation to the lost packet. On lossy mobile links this regularly causes visible page-load stalls.

**2. Slow connection setup.** Opening a secure HTTP/2 connection requires a TCP three-way handshake (1 RTT) followed by a TLS handshake (1 RTT for TLS 1.2; reduced to 1 RTT or 0-RTT with TLS 1.3). For a transcontinental path at 80 ms RTT that is 160 ms before the first byte of content — a substantial fraction of the entire perceived page-load time.

**3. Connection migration.** TCP ties a connection to a 4-tuple: (src IP, src port, dst IP, dst port). Switching from Wi-Fi to cellular changes the source IP, which tears the connection. Every modern mobile user experiences this when leaving a coffee shop.

**QUIC** (Quick UDP Internet Connections) was originally prototyped by **Jim Roskind** at Google in 2012 and deployed experimentally in Chrome in 2013. After years of large-scale production use at Google, the IETF standardized it as **RFC 9000** (May 2021). QUIC solves all three problems:
- Runs over **UDP** (not TCP), so each QUIC stream is independently ordered; a packet loss on stream A does not block stream B.
- Integrates **TLS 1.3** (RFC 8446, 2018) natively — the QUIC handshake and the TLS handshake happen in the same 1-RTT exchange, or **0-RTT** for resumed connections using cached session tickets.
- Uses **connection IDs** (64+ bits) rather than IP/port tuples, so the connection survives a network change.

**Why UDP?** Middleboxes — NATs, firewalls, deep-packet-inspection appliances — are deeply specialized to TCP semantics. Changing TCP itself would require upgrading every middlebox on the internet, a process that would take many years (the "ossification" problem documented by researchers including **Ian Swett**, **Jana Iyengar**, and **Martin Thomson**). UDP is a thin datagram shim over IP with almost no semantics, so QUIC can build exactly the transport it needs on top without negotiating with middleboxes. QUIC's own congestion control and reliability layers handle everything TCP's kernel stack used to manage.

slides.title: HTTP/3 = HTTP semantics over QUIC
slides.body:
**HTTP/3** (RFC 9114, June 2022) is the mapping of HTTP semantics onto QUIC streams. From the application's perspective, HTTP/3 uses the same methods (GET, POST, PUT…), status codes, and header semantics as HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2. The difference is entirely in the transport layer beneath.

**Stream multiplexing without HoL blocking.** Each HTTP request/response pair occupies its own QUIC stream. A dropped UDP packet only affects the stream carrying that packet's data. The server can continue pushing responses on all other streams while the lost packet is retransmitted — a fundamental improvement over HTTP/2 over TCP on any network with non-trivial loss.

**Faster connection setup.**
- *New connection:* 1 RTT for combined QUIC+TLS 1.3 handshake (compared to 2 RTT for TCP + TLS 1.2 HTTP/2).
- *Resumed connection (0-RTT):* Client sends application data alongside the first packet using a cached session ticket. The server can respond before the handshake completes. **0-RTT has a replay-attack caveat** — the server must treat 0-RTT requests as idempotent (safe to re-execute if replayed); POST mutations should not use 0-RTT.

**Connection migration.** A mobile client moving between Wi-Fi and cellular sends the same connection ID from the new IP. The server (e.g., a **Cloudflare** edge node or a **Google** front-end) recognizes the connection ID and continues without re-handshaking. This makes video calls and long downloads seamless across network changes.

**Deployment reality (2024–2025).** Google has served traffic over QUIC since 2013 and HTTP/3 since its standardization. **Cloudflare** enables HTTP/3 by default for all customers. **Meta** (Facebook, Instagram) adopted HTTP/3 to reduce mobile latency. Browser support is universal: Chrome, Firefox, Safari, and Edge all negotiate HTTP/3 via the `Alt-Svc` header or HTTPS DNS records. Industry measurements (Fastly, Cloudflare) show 10–20% latency improvement on lossy mobile connections and up to 30% on very high-loss paths.

**Enterprise caveat.** Some corporate firewalls block UDP port 443, preventing QUIC negotiation. Clients fall back automatically to HTTP/2 over TCP via the `Alt-Svc` mechanism — no user-visible error, just the slower path. The **IETF QUIC working group** (co-chaired by **Mark Nottingham** and others) addressed this fallback in the RFC.

slides.title: QUIC's transport internals — streams, frames, congestion, and loss recovery
slides.body:
QUIC builds a complete, reliable, multiplexed transport protocol on top of the unreliable UDP datagram service. Understanding its internal structure explains both its performance characteristics and its design trade-offs.

**Streams and frames.** A QUIC connection carries multiple **streams** — independent ordered byte sequences, each with its own stream ID. Streams can be unidirectional or bidirectional. Within a stream, data is carried in **STREAM frames** embedded in UDP packets. A single UDP packet may contain frames belonging to multiple streams. QUIC also defines ACK frames, CRYPTO frames (TLS handshake data), CONNECTION_CLOSE frames, and others. This frame-based design is more flexible than TCP's monolithic byte stream.

**Packet numbers.** Unlike TCP sequence numbers (which track byte offsets), QUIC uses monotonically increasing packet numbers that never repeat. This eliminates the "TCP retransmission ambiguity" problem identified by **Phil Karn** (Karn's algorithm, 1987) — retransmitted QUIC packets get new packet numbers, so the sender can always tell whether an ACK refers to the original or the retransmit.

**Loss recovery and acknowledgment.** QUIC's loss-recovery specification is in **RFC 9002** (2021). It uses RACK-style (Recent ACKnowledgment) loss detection: a packet is declared lost when a threshold number of subsequent packets have been ACKed, rather than relying purely on duplicate ACKs as TCP Reno did. This gives faster loss detection on modern high-bandwidth paths.

**Congestion control.** RFC 9002 specifies a default algorithm resembling **TCP NewReno** (RFC 6582), but QUIC explicitly allows pluggable congestion controllers. Google's production QUIC deployment uses **BBR** (Bottleneck Bandwidth and Round-trip propagation time), developed by **Neal Cardwell**, **Yuchung Cheng**, **Matt Mathis**, and colleagues at Google (published 2016). BBR models the network's bottleneck bandwidth and minimum RTT separately, rather than inferring congestion from packet loss, giving better throughput on high-BDP and lightly-lossy links.

**TLS 1.3 integration.** QUIC does not use TLS as a separate layer; it uses TLS 1.3's record protocol for key derivation and certificate exchange but replaces TLS's record layer entirely with QUIC's own packet protection (AEAD — Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data). This means every QUIC packet (except the very first few) is fully encrypted including most header fields, frustrating middlebox inspection. **Martin Thomson** and **Sean Turner** co-authored **RFC 9001** (2021) specifying this integration.

**Connection migration in detail.** When a client's IP changes, it sends a PATH_CHALLENGE frame on a new path. The server responds with PATH_RESPONSE on that path. Once validated, the client migrates the connection, generating new connection IDs as needed to prevent linkability across paths. Connection IDs are rotated to prevent tracking across migrations.

**Practical performance numbers.** Google's 2017 SIGCOMM paper ("QUIC: A UDP-Based Multiplexed and Secure Transport" by **Adam Langley**, **Alistair Riddoch**, **Alyssa Wilk**, and colleagues) reported 3% improvement in mean page-load time and 30% reduction in rebuffer rate for YouTube. On very lossy cellular links (3–5% loss) the improvements are larger, as the independent-stream design avoids the compounding effect of HoL blocking on multiple simultaneous resources.

question.question: Why QUIC avoids head-of-line blocking
question.goal: HTTP/2 over TCP with 4 multiplexed streams. One packet drops. What happens to the others?

steps.prompt: TCP delivers bytes in order. So if a packet is lost, all subsequent bytes (across all multiplexed streams) wait for retransmit. How does QUIC differ?

options: Each QUIC stream has its own byte-stream ordering. A drop on stream A doesn't block stream B's delivery.

hints: QUIC's streams are independent; TCP's are not.
steps.reveal: QUIC streams are independent. Each maintains its own ordering. A packet drop only blocks the stream the lost data belongs to; other streams keep delivering.

question.finalResult: QUIC's signature improvement over HTTP/2 over TCP: independent streams = no head-of-line blocking across streams. On lossy networks (mobile, transcontinental), this dramatically improves throughput.

question.question: QUIC supports connection migration: switching networks (Wi-Fi → cellular) without breaking the connection. The key enabler:
options: QUIC connections are identified by a 64-bit connection ID instead of (IP, port) tuples.
question.explanation: TCP ties a connection to (src IP, src port, dst IP, dst port). Switching networks changes src IP → breaks connection. QUIC uses a connection ID independent of IP — switching networks just sends packets with the same connection ID from the new IP. Server recognizes the connection + continues.

hints: TCP connection identifier vs QUIC connection identifier.
If the identifier doesn't depend on IP, what happens when IP changes?
slides.workedSolution: QUIC's connection-ID-based identification severs the connection's identity from network identity. When a mobile device switches from Wi-Fi to cellular, its IP changes but the QUIC connection ID stays the same. Server recognizes the connection + keeps it alive. Important for mobile UX: video calls, gaming, long-running downloads don't break on network switch.

question.question: Enterprise firewall blocks QUIC
question.prompt: Your video-call app uses QUIC. A user reports it doesn't work on their corporate Wi-Fi. Walk through why this happens + what fallback strategy is standard.
Explain in two or three sentences why QUIC is built on UDP rather than as an upgrade to TCP.
question.rubric: Mentions that the internet's middleboxes (NATs, firewalls, LBs) deeply assume TCP semantics; changing TCP requires internet-wide upgrade (decades); UDP is a thin shim that doesn't constrain QUIC's design; QUIC builds its own reliability + flow control on top.
